title: Scores, cut-offs and ranked lists
subtitle: The model gives a score. Who decides where to cut, and how do you judge the ranking?
goal: After this lesson you can turn a model's scores into a list sized for the team, compare it fairly with a baseline, and say in one sentence what an AUC means.

predict.q: At the default cut-off of 0.5 the model flags 141 advertisers and catches about 20 percent of the churners. Lower the cut-off to 0.2 and it flags 690. What share of the churners does it catch now?
options: About 25 percent
About 40 percent
About 60 percent
About 90 percent
predict.reveal: About 60 percent, three times as many, while precision falls from about 74 to about 46 percent. The lesson shows how to choose that trade.

segments.narration: Last lesson's model caught one churner in five, and the account lead is back with a fair question: can it be less timid? It can, without retraining anything. The model never said yes or no. It gave each of the 4,000 test advertisers a score between zero and one, and a line at 0.5 turned those scores into flags. That line was a default in the code. Nobody in your business chose it. So the question is not what the model flags. It is where you want the line. That holds for any yes-or-no model, whether it scores churn risk or who will adopt the video format.

visual.title: Scores, cut-offs and ranked lists
visual.sub: Nobody said the cut-off had to be 0.5

segments.narration: [[1]] At 0.5 the model flagged 141 advertisers. Precision was about 74 percent and recall about 20. [[2]] Now slide the line down to 0.2. The model flags 690 advertisers. Recall triples, to about 60 percent: three churners in five now get a call. Precision drops to about 46 percent, so more than half the calls are false alarms. Nothing about the model changed: same scores, same order. You moved a line, and traded precision for recall. The assistant's code will call that line a threshold.

visual.title: Same model, same scores, two cut-offs

segments.narration: Every test advertiser's real score is loaded, and the cut-off is yours to drag. Start at 0.5, then pull it down and watch the four counts change. Three things to find. The cut-off that catches nine churners in ten, and how many advertisers it flags. The cut-off where nine flags in ten are right, and how many flags are left. And the cut-off that flags about as many advertisers as the hand rule did. You will not find one that makes precision and recall both high. That is the trade you are choosing. Try it now.

visual.name: threshold
visual.title: Drag the cut-off over the real test scores
visual.note: Find the cut-off that catches 9 churners in 10, the one where 9 flags in 10 are right, and the one that flags about 711, the size of the hand rule's list.

segments.narration: Here is what the slider shows. Nine churners in ten: a cut-off of 0.05, with nearly half of all advertisers flagged. Nine right flags in ten: 0.7, with only 43 flagged. The hand rule's list size: just under 0.2. [[4]] In practice a list length is easier to pick than a cut-off. If account managers can call 200 advertisers, sort by score and take the top 200. In SQL terms: order by score descending, limit 200. The assistant will call it a top K list. It holds 136 churners, 68 percent: that share is called precision at K. A random list would hold about 26, so this one is about five times richer. That ratio is called lift. The churner count wobbles too: on other test advertisers it could be anywhere from 123 to 150.

visual.title: Sort by score, take the top K

segments.narration: Earlier the bar was set: beat the hand rule with the same number of flags. Here is why. The rule flagged 711 advertisers and the default cut-off 141, so comparing their precision compares a long list with a short one, and a short list usually looks more precise. Give both the same length. [[1]] The rule's 711 advertisers hold 246 churners. [[2]] The model's top 711 hold 321. Same effort for the team, more churners reached, and the model is ahead on precision and recall at once. Here the model wins; elsewhere a rule might. Either way, the only fair comparison is at the same list size.

What you are judging, then, is the ranking. Sort all 4,000 test advertisers by score and cut the list into ten equal slices. [[1]] In the top slice, 55 percent churned. [[2]] In the second, about 30 percent. [[3]] In the third, about 14. [[4]] In the fourth, 12, already below the overall average of about 13. A good ranking looks like that: churners piled at the top, almost none at the bottom. The top two slices, a fifth of all advertisers, hold about 64 percent of the churners.

visual.title: Churn rate by slice of the ranked list (400 advertisers each)
visual.note: Test-month average: 13.2%. Six more slices follow, down to 0.5%.

segments.narration: One number sums up a ranking with no cut-off involved: AUC, short for area under the curve. Pick one advertiser who churned and one who stayed, at random. AUC is how often the churner has the higher score. A coin flip gives 0.5. A perfect ranking gives 1. This model gets about 0.85: in 85 pairs out of a hundred, the churner comes out on top. If a report draws the curve, hugging the top left corner is good and the diagonal is the coin flip. Now what AUC hides. It averages over the whole list, so it says little about the top 200, the only part your team will touch. And it only checks order, so it cannot tell you whether a score of 0.3 really means 30 percent.

visual.text: AUC: pick one churner and one stayer at random. How often does the churner have the higher score?
visual.sub: 0.5 = a coin · 1 = perfect · this model: 0.845 · reports draw it as the ROC curve

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Ask the assistant for a score for every test advertiser, never just a yes or no. [[2]] Ask for precision and recall at several cut-offs, not one. [[3]] Ask for the top of the list at sizes your team could handle, with the count a random list would hold beside it. Then the evidence. [[4]] Every precision or recall figure must name the cut-off or list size behind it. [[5]] Any claim that the model beats a baseline must be made at the same list size. And AUC goes in the report on the test months, beside the top of the list, never instead of it.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Ask: a score per advertiser, not a yes or no
Ask: precision and recall at several cut-offs
Ask: top 100, 200, 400, 800 with the random-list count
Check: every figure names its cut-off or list size
Check: model and baseline at the same list size

segments.narration: So when someone needs a list, ask how many the team can handle, take that many from the top, and judge any rival at the same size. So far the score has only been an order. Next lesson: can it be read as a percentage?

takeaways: A model outputs scores; where to cut is your decision, usually set by capacity or cost.
Compare a model and a rule at the same list size, never at different ones.
AUC is how often a random churner outscores a random stayer: it judges the ranking, not the top of the list and not the percentages.

quiz.q: The retention team can call 400 advertisers this month. The assistant's report uses the default cut-off of 0.5 and lists 141. The team lead says: 'The model only gives us 141 names, so we will fill the other 259 from the old rule.' What do you tell her?
options: Good plan: the model has no view on anyone below 0.5, so the rule should fill the gap.
Take the model's top 400 by score: the 0.5 line was a default, not part of the model.
Ask the assistant to retrain until at least 400 advertisers score above the 0.5 line.
Call only the 141: everyone else is predicted to stay, so more calls would be wasted.
quiz.why: Every advertiser has a score, so the list can be any length: the top 400 by score hold 220 churners. Scoring below 0.5 does not mean 'predicted safe', only lower on the same ranking, so the model has an opinion about all 4,000. Retraining to push scores over an arbitrary line fixes nothing.

quiz.concept: compare at the same list size
quiz.q: The assistant's summary says: 'The model clearly beats the hand rule: precision 73.8 percent against 34.6 percent.' The same output shows that the model flagged 141 advertisers and the rule 711. What is the flaw?
options: It should have compared false alarms: 37 for the model against 465 for the rule.
It should have compared recall: 19.7 against 46.7 percent shows the rule is better.
It should have compared accuracy, 88.5 against 81.4 percent, which uses all four boxes.
The lists differ in length: compare the rule with the model's top 711 instead.
quiz.why: A list of 141 and a list of 711 are different jobs for the team, and a short list from a ranking usually looks more precise than a long one. At the same size the model holds 321 churners against the rule's 246, and that is the claim the evidence supports. Switching to recall, to false alarms or to accuracy still sets a short list against a long one.

quiz.q: A lead-scoring model is reported with an AUC of 0.80. The sales manager says: 'So 80 percent of the leads it flags will convert.' What is the right read?
options: No: a random converter outscores a random non-converter 80 percent of the time.
Yes, roughly: AUC is the model's precision averaged over every possible cut-off.
No: it means the model puts 80 percent of all leads on the right side of the cut-off.
No: it means the model catches 80 percent of the leads that go on to convert.
quiz.why: AUC describes the ranking: how often a converter is placed above a non-converter. It is not precision, accuracy or recall, each of which needs a cut-off, so the share of a flagged list that converts has to be read from a top-K table. When few leads convert, that share can sit far below 80 percent even with a good AUC.

quiz.concept: moving the cut-off is a trade
quiz.q: A stakeholder asks for a cut-off that 'catches 90 percent of churners and is right at least 70 percent of the time'. The assistant's table shows recall reaches 90 percent only at a cut-off of 0.05, where precision is 24 percent, and precision passes 70 percent only at 0.5, where recall is 20 percent. What do you reply?
options: Use a cut-off halfway between the two, which should land close to both targets.
Flag only advertisers who clear both cut-offs, 0.05 and 0.5, so both targets are met.
No cut-off on these scores does both: pick the trade by cost and by team capacity.
Rebalance the training data to half churners, so precision and recall rise together.
quiz.why: Moving the cut-off slides along one trade-off: recall is bought with precision, and on these scores the two targets never meet. A halfway cut-off gives roughly half of each, not both, and clearing both cut-offs is just the 0.5 cut-off again. Only a model that ranks better would shift the whole trade, and rebalancing does not do that, so the reply is a choice driven by what a miss and a false alarm cost.

variants.q: A traffic-quality model scores every publisher from 0 to 1 for likely invalid traffic. At the default cut-off of 0.5 it flags 30 publishers. The review team can audit 150 publishers a week. What should the weekly list be?
options: The 30 flagged publishers: the rest are predicted clean.
The 150 highest-scoring publishers: capacity sets the length.
The 30 flagged, plus 120 picked at random for fairness.
Whatever a cut-off of 0.25 produces, since that is half the default.
variants.why: The score ranks every publisher, so the team's capacity sets the list length: sort and take the top 150. The 0.5 line is a default, not a verdict, and publishers below it are simply lower on the same ranking. Random picks or an arbitrary new cut-off throw that ranking away.

variants.q: An upsell model's list has 300 accounts, and 40 percent of them bought. The sales team's own rule produced a list of 1,200 accounts, and 25 percent bought. A manager concludes that the model is better. What is missing?
options: The buyers as counts: 120 on the model's list against 300 on the rule's.
The accuracy of each list, which also counts the accounts left off it.
A comparison at one size: the model's top 1,200 against the rule's 1,200.
A second month of results: one month of lists is too few to compare.
variants.why: A list of 300 and a list of 1,200 are different jobs, and a short list from a ranking usually has the higher hit rate. The rule found 300 buyers; the question is how many buyers sit in the model's top 1,200. Only at equal size do you learn which finds more for the same effort. Setting 120 buyers against 300 is the same unequal comparison written as counts.

variants.q: After a staffing cut, the retention team can call 100 advertisers a month instead of 400. The model is unchanged. What should you expect when the list shrinks from the top 400 to the top 100?
options: Precision rises and recall falls: a shorter list is purer and reaches fewer churners.
Precision and recall both fall, because the model is now applied to fewer advertisers.
Both stay where they were: precision and recall belong to the model, not to the list.
Recall rises and precision falls: the calls are now focused on the likeliest churners.
variants.why: The scores and their order stay the same; only the cut moves up the list. On the course data the top 400 are 55 percent churners and reach about 42 percent of all churners, while the top 100 are 76 percent churners and reach about 14 percent. Precision and recall describe a model plus a cut-off, never the model alone.

review.concept: what AUC means and what it hides

variants.q: A model that scores support tickets for urgency has an AUC of 0.90. Which statement is true?
options: Of the tickets it flags as urgent, 90 percent really are urgent when a person checks.
It finds 90 percent of all the urgent tickets in the inbox and misses one in ten.
It gives the correct label, urgent or not, to 90 percent of all the tickets.
A random urgent ticket outscores a random non-urgent one 90 percent of the time.
variants.why: AUC is about pairs: take one urgent and one non-urgent ticket at random, and it is the chance the urgent one scores higher. The other three statements are precision, recall and accuracy, and each of those needs a cut-off that AUC never uses.

variants.q: Two models rank creatives by risk of fatigue. Model X has an AUC of 0.88 and model Y 0.86. The design team can refresh only the 200 highest-ranked creatives. In the top 200, X has 80 that really fatigued and Y has 124. Which do you use?
options: X: the higher AUC means the better ranking everywhere.
Y: the team only uses the top 200, and Y is better there.
Either: a gap of 0.02 in AUC means the two lists are the same.
Neither, until one of them reaches an AUC of 0.90 or more.
variants.why: AUC averages ranking quality over the whole list, including the many creatives nobody will act on. The decision uses only the top 200, so judge the top 200: 124 against 80. A slightly higher AUC promises nothing about any one part of the list.

variants.q: By mistake, the assistant's script divides every churn score by two before reporting. What happens to the AUC and to the top-200 list?
options: Both get worse, because the scores are now wrong.
The AUC halves; the top-200 list is unchanged.
Neither changes: both depend only on the order of the scores.
The AUC is unchanged, but the list shrinks to a top 100.
variants.why: Halving every score keeps every advertiser in the same order, and AUC and a top-K list use nothing but the order. That is exactly why AUC cannot tell you whether scores are right as percentages: they have all just been cut in half, and AUC did not notice.

drill.q: A model gives every customer a score between zero and one. Who decides where the cut-off goes, and how?
drill.a: You do, not the model. Usually by capacity: sort by score and take as many as the team can handle. The halfway line is only a default in the code.

drill.q: What does an AUC of zero point eight five mean in plain words, and what does it not tell you?
drill.a: Pick one churner and one stayer at random: eighty-five times in a hundred, the churner has the higher score. It measures ranking only. It does not tell you how good the top of the list is, or whether the scores are right as percentages.

recall.prompt: The report says the model's precision is 74 percent and the hand rule's is 35 percent. Explain why that comparison is unfair, how to make it fair, and what single number sums up the ranking.
recall.model_answer: The model's figure is for 141 flagged advertisers and the rule's for 711, and a short list from a ranking usually looks more precise, so the two are not comparable. Sort by score and take the model's top 711: it holds 321 churners against the rule's 246, which is the fair comparison. To sum up the ranking in one number use AUC, the chance that a random churner outscores a random stayer, about 0.85 here. Read the top of the list as well, because AUC averages over everyone.

ask_assistant: Output a score for every test row, not a yes or no. Show a table of number flagged, precision and recall at [several cut-offs across the range]. Show the top [list sizes my team could handle] by score, with the number of real [outcome] cases on each list and the number a random list of that size would hold. Compare the model with my rule [rule] at the rule's own list size, on the same test rows. Report AUC on [the test period] beside these tables, not instead of them, and print the test row count and [outcome] rate.
audit_checklist: Every precision or recall figure names the cut-off or list size it belongs to.
The model and the baseline are compared at the same number flagged.
Each top-K row shows what a random list of that size would hold.
AUC is stated for the test months and sits beside the top-of-list numbers, not in place of them.
transfer: Which leads should sales call first, when the team can make 50 calls a day?
Which publishers should the traffic-quality team audit this week?
Which creatives should be refreshed first, before they fatigue?

other_ways.approach: Set the cut-off from costs: the value of a catch against the cost of a false alarm
other_ways.when: When you can put dollars on both and the percentages can be trusted; a later lesson does this.

other_ways.approach: Two cut-offs and three bands: act now, watch, leave alone
other_ways.when: When you have a cheap action and an expensive one for the same list.

other_ways.approach: A precision-recall summary in place of AUC
other_ways.when: When the outcome is very rare and only the top of the list matters; it weights the top more heavily.

glossary.def: The score above which a row is flagged; a decision you make, not something the model learns.
The K highest-scoring rows: a list sized by what the team can handle, judged against what a random list of that size would hold.
The share of the top K rows that really have the outcome: 136 churners in the top 200 is 68 percent.
How many times richer a list is in the outcome than a random list of the same size: about five times for the top 200 here.
The chance that a randomly chosen positive case scores higher than a randomly chosen negative one; 0.5 is a coin, 1 is perfect.
The chart behind AUC: the closer the line hugs the top-left corner the better the ranking, and the diagonal is a coin flip.
